def: A purine analog chemotherapy drug that inhibits DNA synthesis, used in chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
The modified methionine that starts protein synthesis in bacteria and in mitochondria. Eukaryotic cytoplasmic translation starts with unmodified methionine.
A prodrug of amprenavir, an HIV protease inhibitor that blocks cleavage of viral polyproteins.
An oral inhibitor of spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) that reduces antibody-mediated platelet destruction. It is used in chronic immune thrombocytopenia.
Relating to the forehead and nose. The frontonasal prominence is an embryonic facial swelling that forms the forehead, nose bridge and philtrum.
An antimicrobial that inhibits methionine aminopeptidase 2, used against microsporidia infections.
The superficial layer of the endometrium that thickens under estrogen and progesterone and is shed in menstruation. The deeper basalis layer regenerates it.
Describing a tumor that grows outward in a cauliflower-like mass, often ulcerating and prone to bleeding or infection.
Galactose in the urine, a feature of galactosemia caused by a deficiency of galactose-metabolizing enzymes.
The blood protein fraction on electrophoresis that mostly consists of antibodies (immunoglobulins). A sharp spike in this region suggests a monoclonal gammopathy such as myeloma.
The herpesvirus subfamily that infects lymphocytes and includes Epstein-Barr virus (HHV-4) and Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (HHV-8).
A surgical connection between the stomach and the jejunum, used to bypass gastric outlet obstruction or in procedures such as Roux-en-Y bypass.
Describing an agent that speeds stomach emptying, such as metoclopramide, used in gastroparesis.
The smooth area of the forehead between the eyebrows, just above the bridge of the nose.
Hairless and smooth. Glabrous skin, such as on the palms and soles, has no hair follicles.
A hepatitis C drug that inhibits the viral NS3/4A protease. It is combined with pibrentasvir in a pan-genotypic regimen.
A sulfonylurea that closes pancreatic beta-cell potassium channels to stimulate insulin release, used in type 2 diabetes. Hypoglycemia is the main risk.
A glycolipid (Gb3) that accumulates in Fabry disease because alpha-galactosidase A is deficient, damaging kidneys, heart and nerves.
Resembling a kidney glomerulus. Glomeruloid vascular proliferation, tufts of abnormal capillaries, is a feature of glioblastoma.
Describing the bond that links a sugar to another molecule, such as the bonds joining sugars in starch and glycogen or a sugar to a nucleotide base.
Substances that interfere with thyroid hormone production and can cause a goiter, such as cassava and certain cruciferous vegetables, or drugs such as lithium.
A monoclonal antibody against TNF-alpha used for rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and ulcerative colitis.
A hepatitis C drug that inhibits the NS3/4A protease, given with elbasvir.
The segmented pouch-like appearance of the colon wall. Loss of haustra on imaging suggests long-standing ulcerative colitis.
The opening at the apex of the cochlea where the scala vestibuli and scala tympani join.
A violet-colored rash on the upper eyelids, characteristic of dermatomyositis.
Blood collecting in the fallopian tube, which can occur with tubal pregnancy or endometriosis.
Loss of half of the visual field in each eye, caused by a lesion behind the optic chiasm. Its location determines the pattern, such as homonymous hemianopia.
A vein on the left side of the posterior chest wall that drains the left posterior intercostal spaces and crosses to empty into the azygos vein.
Relating to hemidesmosomes, which anchor basal epithelial cells to the basement membrane via integrins. Autoantibodies against them cause bullous pemphigoid.
Damage to one half of the spinal cord, producing Brown-Sequard syndrome with ipsilateral motor and proprioceptive loss and contralateral pain and temperature loss.
Free hemoglobin in the plasma, seen with intravascular hemolysis and causing pink plasma.
A protein that promotes hepcidin production in the liver. Mutations cause juvenile hemochromatosis.
Blood in the middle ear behind the eardrum, which looks blue-purple and is a sign of basilar skull fracture.
A copper-containing ferroxidase on intestinal cells that oxidizes iron so transferrin can carry it into the blood.
The salt of hippuric acid, formed in the liver from benzoate and glycine and excreted in urine. Some bacteria, like group B streptococcus, are identified by hippurate hydrolysis.
A muscarinic antagonist used as eye drops to dilate the pupil and paralyze accommodation, and in cough preparations.
